title: Why Some People Have More
bigQuestion: Why do some people and places have more than others, and what makes a chance fair?

story.title: Two Cousins, One Dream
story.kicker: Luis and Marisol are cousins. Both want to be doctors. They live in two different countries.
paragraphs: Luis is eleven. He lives in Chicago. Every morning he rides a yellow bus to school. His school has a science lab and a nurse's office. Luis loves the nurse's office. He wants to be a doctor one day.

His cousin Marisol is also eleven. She lives in a small mountain town in Honduras, in Central America. She walks almost an hour to school. Her class shares a few old books. Marisol wants to be a doctor too.

Both cousins are smart. Both work hard. Both help at home. On Sundays they talk on a video call. Luis shows her a model of a heart from his library. Marisol tells him about the clinic in the next town. It is open only two days a week.
Marisol's family grows coffee. In a good year, they sell a lot. In a year with too little rain, they sell less. Then her parents worry about money for her school shoes and bus rides to high school.
The two cousins have the same dream. They have the same grandparents. Yet the road ahead looks different for each of them. Why is that? This chapter looks for answers.
story.think: Luis and Marisol have the same dream. What things might make that dream easier or harder for each of them?

lessons.title: Income and Wealth
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money you get over time; wealth is everything you own, minus what you owe.
reading: Ms. Park is a bus driver. Every two weeks she gets a paycheck. That paycheck is her *income*. Income is money that comes in over time. It can come from a job, a business or other places.

Ms. Park also owns things. She has a small house, a car and some money in the bank. All that she owns, minus what she owes, is her *wealth*. If she still owes money on her house, that part is not really hers yet.

Income and wealth are not the same. A person can earn a good income but own little. Another person can own a farm but have a small income this year. Both words help us understand who has more, and why.

words.d: money that comes in over time, like pay from a job
everything a person owns, minus what they owe

look.title: Sort It Out
look.text: Look at this list: a weekly paycheck, a house, money earned selling lemonade this summer, a bicycle, a savings account, a tip from a customer.
look.prompt: Which items are income coming in? Which are part of someone's wealth?

check.q: What is income?
choices: Money a person owes the bank
Money that comes in over time, like pay
check.why: Income is money that comes in over time, like a paycheck.

check.q: Ms. Park owns a house and a car and has money in the bank. What word describes all of this, minus what she owes?
check.why: Wealth is everything a person owns, minus what they owe.

check.q: Which statement from the reading is true?
choices: Income and wealth always go together
A person can have a good income but own little
Wealth is only money in a pocket
check.why: The reading says a person can earn a good income but own little.

lessons.title: Saving and Owning
lessons.mainIdea: Saving money and owning things like land or a business can help wealth grow over time.
reading: Mr. Okafor opened a small bakery. First he saved part of his pay for five years. Then he used the savings to rent a shop and buy an oven. Now the bakery earns money every day.

*Saving* means keeping some money instead of spending it now. Savings can be used later to buy things that earn money. A shop, a farm or a building can earn money for years. Things you own that have value are called *assets*.

Wealth often grows when people own assets. A family that owns a home can pass it to its children. That gives the children a head start. A family with no assets starts from zero. This is one reason wealth gaps can last a long time.

words.d: keeping some money to use later instead of spending it now
something you own that has value, like a home, land or a business

look.title: Two Paths for $100
look.text: Ana gets $100 for her birthday. Path 1: she spends it all on a game this week. Path 2: she saves it. Next summer she uses it to buy a used lawn mower. She mows neighbors' lawns and earns $20 each time.
look.prompt: Which path could help Ana earn more money later? Why?

check.q: What is an asset?
choices: Something you own that has value
check.why: An asset is something you own that has value, like a home or a business.

check.q: How did Mr. Okafor start his bakery?
choices: He saved part of his pay for years
He found an oven on the street
check.why: He saved part of his pay for five years, then used the savings to start.

check.q: Why can wealth gaps between families last a long time?
choices: Assets like homes can be passed to children
Banks give money only on Mondays
check.why: Families with assets can pass them down, giving their children a head start.

lessons.title: Training and Pay
lessons.mainIdea: Jobs that need more training or school often pay more, on average.
reading: Dr. Reyes is a nurse practitioner. She studied for about seven years after high school. Her friend works at a store. He started right after high school. On average, Dr. Reyes earns more.

Jobs that need special skills often pay more. The skills take years of *training* or school to learn. Also, fewer people can do those jobs. When something is needed and hard to find, people often pay more for it.

This is an average, not a rule. Some people with little schooling start businesses and earn a lot. Some people with lots of schooling earn little. And many jobs that pay less, like caring for children, are very important. Pay is not the same as value.

words.d: learning the skills needed for a job
a typical amount found by adding numbers and dividing by how many there are

look.title: School and Weekly Pay in the U.S.
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Education Pays, 2023 data
look.prompt: About how much more per week does a typical worker with a four-year degree earn than one with a high school diploma?

check.q: Why do jobs that need special skills often pay more?
choices: The skills take years to learn, and fewer people can do them
The government picks their pay by lottery
check.why: The reading says the skills take years to learn and fewer people can do those jobs.

check.q: In the chart, which group earns the most per week?
check.why: The Master's degree row shows the highest number, about $1,740.

check.q: What does the reading mean by 'Pay is not the same as value'?
choices: Some important jobs, like caring for children, pay less
check.why: The reading says many jobs that pay less, like child care, are very important.

lessons.title: Luck and Where You Are Born
lessons.mainIdea: Luck and the place and family you are born into also shape how much people have.
reading: Remember Luis and Marisol. They are both smart and hard-working. But Luis goes to a school with a lab. Marisol walks an hour to a school with few books. Neither cousin chose where to be born.

*Luck* is what happens to you by chance, not by choice. Being born in a rich country is luck. So is a storm that ruins a farm, or a sickness in the family. Good luck and bad luck can both change a family's money.
Hard work and choices matter a lot. So does luck. Most experts agree that both play a part. People disagree about how much each one counts. That question is part of many debates about fairness.

words.d: things that happen to you by chance, not by your choice
the way things can happen without anyone planning them

look.title: A Storm on the Farm
look.text: Two farmers live side by side. Both plant corn. Both work from sunrise to sunset. In July, a hailstorm crosses the fields. It flattens one farmer's corn. It misses the other farmer's field by a few feet.
look.prompt: Did one farmer work harder than the other? What made the difference?

check.q: What is luck?
choices: Things that happen by chance, not by choice
check.why: Luck is what happens to you by chance, not by your choice.

check.q: In the hailstorm example, why did one farmer lose the corn?
choices: The storm hit his field by chance
check.why: Both worked equally hard; the storm hit one field by chance.

check.q: What does the reading say about hard work and luck?
choices: Both play a part, and people disagree about how much each counts
check.why: The reading says both play a part and people disagree about how much each counts.

lessons.title: Being Poor Is Not Who You Are
lessons.mainIdea: Being poor means having too little money for needs; it is not a sign of a person's worth.
reading: Jada's mom lost her job when her company closed. For a few months, money was very tight. Jada still did her homework. Her mom still made dinner. They were the same kind, hard-working people as before.

Being *poor* means not having enough money for basic needs. *Needs* are things people must have to live, like food, a safe home, clothes and health care. Many families are poor for a while, then things get better.

Being poor does not tell you who a person is. It does not mean they are lazy or less smart. Many causes, like a closed factory, an illness or low pay, can lead to it. Every person deserves respect, whatever their money.

words.d: not having enough money for basic needs
things people must have to live, like food, a safe home, clothes and health care

look.title: What Would You Say?
look.text: At lunch, a student says, 'Kids who get free lunch must have lazy parents.' Another student knows her dad works two jobs. Her family still qualifies for free lunch.
look.prompt: Using the reading, what could someone say to answer the first student kindly and truthfully?

check.q: Which of these is a basic need?
choices: A trip to an amusement park
check.why: Needs are things people must have to live, like a safe home.

check.q: Why did Jada's family have less money for a few months?
choices: They spent it all on toys
check.why: The reading says her mom lost her job when her company closed.

check.q: According to the reading, what does being poor tell you about a person?
choices: That they will always be poor
It does not tell you who they are
check.why: The reading says being poor does not tell you who a person is.

lessons.title: Food Banks and Neighbors
lessons.mainIdea: Food banks and other groups collect food and share it with people who need it.
reading: On Saturday morning, Tom and his dad sort cans at a food pantry. They put beans in one box and soup in another. Later, families come in and choose what they need.

A *food bank* is a big warehouse that collects food. It gets food from farms, stores and people who give. It sends the food to smaller *food pantries* in neighborhoods. Chicago has a large one, the Greater Chicago Food Depository.

Many food banks are run by *charities*, groups that help people and do not try to make a profit. Churches, mosques, temples and neighbors help too. Volunteers give their time. Anyone might need help someday, and anyone can help.

words.d: a big warehouse that collects food and sends it to places that share it
a neighborhood place where families can pick up food they need
a group that helps people and does not try to make a profit

look.title: Follow the Can of Soup
look.text: A farmer grows tomatoes. A company makes them into soup. A grocery store has extra cans. It gives them to the food bank. A truck takes them to a pantry at a church. A grandmother picks up a can for dinner.
look.prompt: Name each stop the soup made. Where could a volunteer help along the way?

check.q: What does a food bank do?
choices: Collects food and sends it to pantries
Sells food for a big profit
check.why: A food bank collects food and sends it to smaller pantries.

check.q: What is a charity?
choices: A group that helps people and does not try to make a profit
check.why: A charity helps people and does not try to make a profit.

check.q: What large food bank does the reading name in Chicago?
check.why: The reading names the Greater Chicago Food Depository.

lessons.title: Schools and Libraries for All
lessons.mainIdea: Public schools and libraries give everyone a chance to learn, no matter how much money they have.
reading: After school, Mei goes to her neighborhood library. She borrows books and uses a computer for homework. It costs her nothing. Her library card is free.

A *public library* is open to everyone and paid for by taxes. *Taxes* are money people and businesses pay to the government for shared services. The Chicago Public Library opened in 1873. Today it has branches all over the city.

Public schools are paid for by taxes too. In the United States, every child can go to school for free. Many people believe free schools and libraries help make chances fairer. A child with no books at home can still read every day.

words.d: a library open to everyone and paid for by taxes
money people and businesses pay to the government for shared services

look.title: A Promise to Every Person
look.text: Everyone has the right to education.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 26, 1948
look.prompt: How do public schools and libraries help keep this promise?

check.q: How are public libraries paid for?
choices: By a fee each time you borrow
check.why: Public libraries are paid for by taxes.

check.q: When did the Chicago Public Library open?
check.why: The reading says the Chicago Public Library opened in 1873.

check.q: Why do many people believe free schools and libraries make chances fairer?
choices: A child with no books at home can still read every day
check.why: The reading says a child with no books at home can still read every day.

lessons.title: Rich and Poor Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Countries differ a lot in wealth, and the share of people in extreme poverty has fallen over time.
reading: In some countries, most homes have running water and electricity. In others, many families carry water from a well. Marisol's town in Honduras has a clinic open two days a week. Luis's city has many hospitals.

Some people live in *extreme poverty*. The World Bank uses that term for living on only a couple of dollars a day. In 1990, more than one in three people in the world lived this way. By 2019, it was about one in ten.

Why did this happen? Many countries grew more food, built factories and sent more children to school. Trade between countries grew too. People still debate which causes mattered most. Hundreds of millions of people still live in extreme poverty.

words.d: living on so little money that it is hard to meet basic needs; the World Bank sets a dollar line for it
buying and selling goods between people or countries

look.title: Share of the World in Extreme Poverty
look.cite: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform estimates ($2.15-a-day line, 2017 prices)
look.prompt: What happened to the share of people in extreme poverty from 1990 to 2019?

check.q: About what share of the world lived in extreme poverty in 1990?
check.why: The reading and chart show about 38 percent, which is more than one in three.

check.q: Which group measured the numbers in the chart?
check.why: The chart cites the World Bank.

check.q: What does the reading say about the causes of the drop in extreme poverty?
choices: There were many causes, and people debate which mattered most
check.why: The reading lists several causes and says people still debate which mattered most.

lessons.title: What Is Fair?
lessons.mainIdea: Opportunity means having a real chance, and people have different ideas about what makes chances fair.
reading: Picture a race. One runner starts at the line. Another starts ten steps behind. Both run hard. Is the race fair? Most people would say no. The runners did not have the same start.

*Opportunity* is a real chance to do something, like go to school or get a good job. *Fairness* means treating people in a way that is right and just. Many people say a fair country gives every child a real opportunity.

People agree on a lot, but not everything. Some say fair means the same rules for everyone. Some say fair means extra help for those who start behind. Many people believe some of both. Good thinkers listen to each side.

words.d: a real chance to do something, like go to school or get a job
treating people in a way that is right and just

look.title: Two Ideas of Fair
look.text: Idea 1: Give every student the same book and the same test. Same rules for all is fair. Idea 2: Give every student the same test, but give a student who needs glasses a pair first. Helping each person reach the start line is fair.
look.prompt: What is good about each idea? When might you use each one?

check.q: What is opportunity?
choices: A real chance to do something
check.why: Opportunity is a real chance to do something, like go to school.

check.q: Why does the race in the reading seem unfair?
choices: One runner starts ten steps behind
check.why: The runners did not have the same start.

check.q: What does the reading say good thinkers do about different ideas of fairness?
check.why: The reading says good thinkers listen to each side.

lessons.title: Different Ideas About Helping
lessons.mainIdea: People disagree about who should help most: families, charities, businesses or the government.
reading: A town has a problem. Some families cannot afford food. The town meets to talk. One neighbor says the church and food pantry should help. Another says the government should run a program. A store owner offers to hire more workers.

People have different ideas about who should help. Some think *government* programs, paid for by taxes, work best for big problems. They say help should reach everyone. Others think families, charities and businesses help best. They say local people know their neighbors' needs.

Each view has supporters and critics. Most countries use a mix. In the United States, food pantries, churches, businesses and government programs all help. Adults debate the right mix at every election.

words.d: the group of people and offices that make and carry out laws for a place
a planned service, like one that helps families buy food

look.title: The Town Meeting
look.text: Speaker 1: 'Our taxes should pay for a food program. Then no family is missed.' Speaker 2: 'Our churches and pantries know each family. They can help faster and with a personal touch.' Speaker 3: 'More jobs in town would help families earn their own money.'
look.prompt: What is one strong point each speaker makes? Could the town use more than one idea?

check.q: What do some people say is good about government programs?
choices: They are run by one family
check.why: Supporters say government programs can reach everyone.

check.q: What do some people say is good about help from charities and neighbors?
choices: They are run by a king
Local people know their neighbors' needs
check.why: Supporters say local people know their neighbors' needs.

check.q: What do most countries do, according to the reading?
choices: Use a mix of ways to help
check.why: The reading says most countries use a mix.

review.q: Which is an example of income?
review.why: Income is money that comes in over time, like a paycheck. The others are things owned.

review.q: What is the difference between a food bank and a food pantry?
choices: A food bank collects food; a pantry shares it with families nearby
A pantry is a warehouse; a bank is a store
A food bank sells food for profit
review.why: A food bank is a big warehouse that sends food to neighborhood pantries.

review.q: Luis and Marisol are both smart and hard-working. What does the story show as a big difference between them?
choices: One does not want to be a doctor
review.why: The story shows they were born in places with different schools and resources.

review.q: Which of these is an asset?
review.why: An asset is something you own that has value, like a business.

review.q: What does the chart from the Bureau of Labor Statistics show?
choices: Workers with more schooling earn more on average
Workers with less school always earn more
Pay has nothing to do with school
review.why: The chart shows typical weekly pay rising with more schooling.

review.q: Which statement about being poor matches the chapter?
choices: It shows a person is lazy
It means you are less smart
It can happen for many reasons and says nothing about a person's worth
review.why: The chapter says many causes can lead to being poor, and every person deserves respect.

review.q: What does 'Everyone has the right to education' come from?
choices: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
review.why: It is from Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, 1948.

review.q: Two people disagree. One says the same rules for all is fair. The other says extra help for those who start behind is fair. What is this debate about?
review.why: Both are talking about what fairness means.
